title: Binary Search on Answer: Split Array Largest Sum
oneLiner: Instead of choosing where to cut, guess the largest allowed part sum and check greedily whether k parts are enough; then binary search the guess.
keyTakeaway: "Minimize the maximum" is usually binary search on the answer. Fix a cap on the part sum: a greedy left-to-right pass tells you the fewest parts that respect it, and that count only goes down as the cap goes up. So the smallest cap needing at most k parts is a boundary you can binary search between max(nums) and sum(nums).
explanation:
Given an array of non-negative integers nums and an integer k (1 <= k <= nums.length), split nums into k non-empty contiguous parts so that the largest part sum is as small as possible, and return that largest sum. For [7, 2, 5, 10, 8] with k = 2 the best split is [7, 2, 5] and [10, 8], giving max(14, 18) = 18.

Trying every set of k - 1 cut positions is exponential. A DP over (prefix, parts used) works in O(k·n²). The faster idea is to turn the question around: instead of asking "where do I cut?", ask "if no part may exceed cap, how many parts do I need?" That second question has a simple greedy answer: walk left to right, adding each number to the current part, and start a new part only when the next number would push the current one over cap. Closing a part as late as possible can never hurt, so this gives the fewest parts for that cap in one O(n) pass.

partsNeeded(cap) is monotonic: a bigger cap never needs more parts. The answer is the smallest cap with partsNeeded(cap) <= k. (Needing fewer than k parts is fine, because you can always split a part further without raising the maximum, as long as there are enough elements, which k <= n guarantees.) The search range is [max(nums), sum(nums)]: below max(nums) the biggest element can't fit in any part, and sum(nums) always works with one part. Binary search it with the same lower-boundary loop as Koko: if partsNeeded(mid) <= k, hi = mid; otherwise lo = mid + 1.

That is O(n log S), where S = sum - max is the size of the answer range, and O(1) extra space. The same shape solves "capacity to ship packages within D days" (identical, with days instead of parts), "painter's partition", and "allocate minimum pages". When you see minimize the maximum (or maximize the minimum, as in "aggressive cows" or "magnetic force between balls"), look for the monotonic feasibility check first.

The visualization shows the candidate caps from 10 to 32 for [7, 2, 5, 10, 8] and k = 2, with the greedy split for each midpoint in the message.

visualizationSteps.message: nums = [7, 2, 5, 10, 8], k = 2. The answer is a cap between max = 10 and sum = 32. Find the smallest cap the greedy split can meet with at most 2 parts.
cap 21: greedy split [7, 2, 5] [10, 8] uses 2 part(s) <= 2. Feasible, try smaller (hi = 21).
cap 15: greedy split [7, 2, 5] [10] [8] needs 3 parts > 2. Too small, try bigger (lo = 16).
cap 18: greedy split [7, 2, 5] [10, 8] uses 2 part(s) <= 2. Feasible, try smaller (hi = 18).
cap 17: greedy split [7, 2, 5] [10] [8] needs 3 parts > 2. Too small, try bigger (lo = 18).
lo == hi == 18. Smallest feasible cap: 18, from the split [7, 2, 5] [10, 8].

recognitionSignals: "Minimize the largest" (or "maximize the smallest") something over all ways to split, assign, or schedule.
Contiguous parts in a fixed order: days, workers, painters, or subarrays that must keep the original order.
Checking one candidate answer is easy (a greedy pass) even though building the best split directly is not.
gotchas: The low end is max(nums), not 0 or 1: with a cap smaller than the biggest element, the greedy check still puts that element in a part of its own and counts it, so it can report a cap as feasible when no valid split exists.
Feasible means partsNeeded(cap) <= k, not == k. Requiring exactly k parts breaks monotonicity and can skip the real answer.
In the greedy check, start a new part when current + x > cap (strictly greater). Using >= closes parts that would have fit exactly and overcounts.
confusableWith: Binary Search on Answer: Minimum Eating Speed (this track) is the same pattern with a different feasibility check (hours needed at speed k). Recognizing that both are "smallest value where a monotonic check flips" is the whole skill.
Dynamic programming over (prefix, parts used) also solves this, in O(k·n²). It's correct and worth mentioning, but the binary search is much faster and simpler to write.

complexity.note: Here m is the size of the answer range, sum(nums) - max(nums). The binary search takes log m steps and each one runs an O(n) greedy pass to count parts.
